reports.text: ARCHIVE: The Israel lobby is the network of pro-Israel groups in Washington. AIPAC is the biggest one. The defense of American policy in Lebanon was always the same. America supports Israel because the American people support Israel. Jennifer Cannata, an AIPAC spokeswoman, said exactly that during the war. After denying the lobby had any influence, she said: "the American people overwhelmingly support Israel's war on terrorism and understand that we must stand by our closest ally in this time of crisis." The polls say she was wrong. On every major question Americans were closer to the rest of the world than to their own government. Who is to blame for starting it? An ABC News-Washington Post poll, August 3 to 6 2006: 46 percent said Israel and Hezbollah were equally to blame. Another 7 percent blamed Israel alone. A CBS News-New York Times poll, July 21 to 25: 46 percent blamed "both sides equally," 5 percent blamed "mostly Israel." Did Israel go too far? USA Today-Gallup, July 21 to 23: 38 percent disapproved of the military action Israel had taken in Lebanon. ABC News-Washington Post: 32 percent said Israel was using "too much force." 48 percent said Israel was "not justified in bombing Hezbollah targets located in areas where civilians may be killed or wounded." 54 percent said Israel "should do more" to avoid civilian casualties. Should America take a side? USA Today-Gallup: 65 percent said the United States should take "neither side." Zogby, August 11 to 15: 52 percent said the US should remain neutral. CBS News-New York Times: 40 percent said the US should "say or do nothing." NBC News-Wall Street Journal, July 21 to 24: 40 percent opposed "U.S. military involvement in support of Israel" if the war expanded. Should there be a cease-fire? CNN, July 19: 43 percent said "Israel should agree to a cease-fire as soon as possible." ABC News-Washington Post: 35 percent said "Israel should agree to an immediate, unconditional cease-fire." Would this hurt America? USA Today-Gallup: 44 percent were "very concerned" that events in Lebanon "will increase the likelihood of terrorism against the United States." 31 percent were somewhat concerned. ABC News-Washington Post: 35 percent said the Lebanon war would "hurt the situation for the United States in Iraq." So there was a sizable gap between what Americans thought and what their leaders did. Mass opinion cannot explain why Bush and Congress acted the way they did in the summer of 2006. Now the other excuse. Some say Israel was just doing America's bidding. A client state. Uri Avnery, the Israeli journalist, called it a war by proxy: Hezbollah is the Dobermann of Iran, and Israel is the Rottweiler of America. That does not fit either. If Israel were doing America's bidding, its bombing would have been confined to southern Lebanon and it would have protected the Lebanese government Bush had worked to install. The United States almost certainly would not have wanted to "turn the clock back in Lebanon by twenty years," as the IDF chief of staff said. Shabtai Shavit ran the Mossad from 1989 to 1996. He said: "We do what we think is best for us, and if it happens to meet America's requirements, that's just part of a relationship between two friends." Moshe Dayan said it best: "Our American friends offer us money, arms, and advice. We take the money, we take the arms, and we decline the advice." And Aaron Miller, a former State Department official, said during the war: "There is a danger in a policy in which there is no daylight whatsoever between the government of Israel and the government of the United States." My analysis is this is the whole answer to the question. The lobby says America backs Israel because Americans back Israel. But 65 percent of Americans wanted no side taken. 54 percent said Israel should do more to avoid civilians. 44 percent were very concerned it would bring more terrorism to America. The American people saw it clearly. Their government did not. And it was not because Israel was America's puppet either. Dayan said it decades ago. We take the money, we take the arms, and we decline the advice. That is the relationship. Not a partnership. Not a client. One country takes what it needs from another and does what it wants. And the lobby makes sure the money and the arms keep coming no matter what the American people say. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The core argument for the special relationship is that Israel is a vital strategic ally. The authors of this book say that argument is false. Here is their conclusion, in their own words. "Although we believe that America should support Israel's existence, Israel's security is ultimately not of critical strategic importance to the United States." Then they explain what would happen if Israel were conquered. "In the event that Israel was conquered—which is extremely unlikely given its considerable military power and its robust nuclear deterrent—neither America's territorial integrity, its military power, its economic prosperity, nor its core political values would be jeopardized." Compare that to oil. "By contrast, if oil exports from the Persian Gulf were significantly reduced, the effects on America's well-being would be profound." So they draw the line clearly. The United States does not support Israel because it makes Americans safer. "The United States does not support Israel's existence because it makes Americans more secure, but rather because Americans recognize the long history of Jewish suffering and believe that it is desirable for the Jewish people to have their own state." They are not saying Israel should be abandoned. They say there is a strong moral case. And the US should remain committed to coming to Israel's aid if its survival were ever in jeopardy. But Americans should do this because they think it is morally appropriate, not because it is vital to their own security. For decades the lobby has sold Israel as a strategic asset. It is the shield of the Middle East. It is the frontline against terrorism. It is America's only real ally in the region. The authors look at that argument and say no. If Israel disappeared tomorrow, America would still be safe. America would still be rich. America would still be free. The only reason to support Israel is moral. That is a good reason. It is an honest reason. But it is a completely different reason than what the lobby has been telling the American people for forty years. And once you admit the strategic case is false, the whole conversation changes. Because then the question is not what Israel does for America. The question is what America owes Israel. And that is a moral question, not a military one. And the lobby does not want you to ask it that way. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: People say the two-state solution is the answer. The problem is the Palestinians. They say Israel wants peace and the other side keeps rejecting it. The polling data says something different. The Israeli public itself rejects every core ingredient of a real peace deal. This is from a 2007 survey, quoted in the book. In principle, 55 percent of Israelis support the establishment of a Palestinian state. That sounds like a majority for peace. But then you get to the details. Only 41 percent support creating a Palestinian state on 95 percent of the West Bank and Gaza, even if Israel was allowed to keep its large settlement blocs.Only 37 percent would support transferring the Arab neighborhoods in East Jerusalem to the Palestinians. Only 22 percent favor transferring control of the Jordan River Valley to a Palestinian state in a few years. Only 27 percent support giving control of the Temple Mount to the Palestinians, with Israel retaining control of the Western Wall. And only 17 percent favor allowing even a limited number of refugees to return to Israel. 17 percent. Not a full right of return. A limited number. And 83 percent of Israeli Jews say no. So the majority supports "a Palestinian state" in the abstract. But when you get to what a Palestinian state would actually require, the support collapses. Every one of those five issues is a core final-status issue. Every one of them is rejected by a majority of Israeli Jews. This is the part nobody wants to say out loud. The two-state solution is dead not because the Palestinians reject it. It is dead because the Israeli public rejects every single thing it would take to make it real. You cannot have a state on 95 percent of the West Bank if only 41 percent of Israelis support it. You cannot have a capital in East Jerusalem if only 37 percent support it. You cannot resolve the refugee issue with 17 percent. And then when the deal does not happen, the lobby blames the Palestinians and the world believes it. But look at the numbers. This is what the Israeli public actually wants. And then they wonder why there is no peace. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: People say the two-state solution is impossible. Maybe it is. But then what? The authors of this book lay out the three alternatives. None of them are good. And the people who oppose two states never say which one they actually want. The first alternative is ethnic cleansing. Israel could expel the Palestinians from its pre-1967 lands and from the Occupied Territories. That would preserve Israel Jewish character through an overt act of expulsion. The authors say some Israeli hard-liners, including Deputy Prime Minister Avigdor Lieberman, have advocated variants of this approach. Their verdict is blunt. To do so "would be a crime against humanity and no genuine friend of Israel could support such a heinous course of action." They add: if this is what opponents of a two-state solution are advocating, they should say so explicitly. The second alternative is a binational state. Instead of separate Jewish and Palestinian states, all of Mandate Palestine becomes one democratic state where both peoples have equal political rights. A handful of Jews and a growing number of Israeli Arabs have suggested this. But the authors say the practical obstacles are daunting, binational states do not have an encouraging track record, and this option means abandoning the original Zionist vision of a Jewish state. There is little reason to think Israel Jewish citizens would accept it. The third alternative is apartheid. Israel continues to increase its control over the Occupied Territories but allows the Palestinians limited autonomy in a set of disconnected and economically crippled statelets. The authors say Israelis bristle at the comparison to white rule in South Africa. But that is the future they face if they try to control all of Mandate Palestine while denying full political rights to an Arab population that will soon outnumber the Jewish population in the entirety of the land. And apartheid is not a long-term solution either. It is morally repugnant. The Palestinians will continue to resist until they get a state of their own. This will force Israel to escalate repressive policies that have already cost it significant blood and treasure, encouraged political corruption, and badly tarnished its global image. My analysis is this is the question the lobby never answers. Every time someone says make a Palestinian state, the lobby says no, it is too dangerous, the Palestinians are terrorists, there is no partner. Okay. So then what is your plan? Expel them? That is a crime against humanity and even the authors say no genuine friend of Israel could support it. One binational state? That destroys the Jewish state. Apartheid? That is South Africa. And we all know how South Africa ended. So the lobby has no plan. It just says no to the only plan that works and pretends the other options do not exist. That is not a strategy. That is a stall. And the price of that stall is paid by Palestinians every day and by Israel in the long run. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # Palestine # Apartheid # MiddleEast

ARCHIVE: AIPAC and the Conference of Presidents claim to speak for Jews. Not just American Jews. Jews everywhere. And when they say a policy is what Jews want, politicians believe them. But Jews in other countries have started saying no. You do not speak for us. February 2007: a group of British Jews founded Independent Jewish Voices. It favors the universal application of human rights law and a negotiated peace between Israelis and Palestinians. It condemns anti-Semitism, anti-Arabism, and Islamophobia. Its founding declaration said it exists "in the belief that the broad spectrum of opinion among the Jewish population of this country is not reflected by those institutions which claim authority to represent the Jewish community as a whole." The declaration added: "the battle against anti-Semitism is vital and is undermined whenever opposition to Israeli government policies is automatically branded as anti-Semitic." In Australia, Jews who are critical of Israeli policy and found it difficult to voice their views formed an organization called Independent Australian Jewish Voices. November 2006: twenty-five peace researchers in Germany called for questioning the "special relationship" between Germany and Israel because of Israel actions against the Palestinians. March 2007: a heated controversy broke out within the German Jewish community. A small group of Jews issued the "Berlin Declaration Shalom 5767." According to the Forward it criticized Israeli policy in the Occupied Territories and "the limits of open debate on matters in relation to the Middle East." In the United States too, groups like the Israel Policy Forum, Brit Tzedek v'Shalom, and Americans for Peace Now have become more visible and effective. They were reportedly pondering a merger to enhance their influence and encourage greater US effort toward a two-state solution. A number of prominent American Jews had also considered founding a new lobbying group as a reasonable alternative to AIPAC. And here is the part that matters. The authors write: "Initiatives like these remind us that the policy positions espoused by the most influential groups in the lobby do not represent the views of all (or even most) diaspora Jews." The answer to the antisemitism charge:When the lobby says you are attacking Jews, ask them which Jews. Because Jews in London, in Sydney, in Berlin, in Washington are organizing against the lobby's positions. They are saying the hard-liners do not speak for them. And the British group said the most important thing. Every time opposition to Israeli policy gets branded as antisemitic, real antisemitism gets weaker. Because the word stops meaning anything. So the lobby's favorite weapon is not just silencing debate. It is damaging the fight against actual hatred of Jews. And the people saying that out loud now are Jews themselves. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # HumanRights # MiddleEast # Palestine

ARCHIVE: If the lobby were the path to peace, then the presidents who listened to it most should have made the most peace. The opposite happened. The two presidents who made the greatest contribution to Middle East peace were Jimmy Carter and George H. W. Bush. Carter brokered the Egypt-Israel treaty at Camp David in 1979. Bush Sr. pressured Israel over the loan guarantees in 1991 and 1992, which opened the way for the Madrid Conference that brought Arabs and Israelis to the table for the first time. And why were they able to do it? The authors quote the former Israeli foreign minister Shlomo Ben-Ami. "Carter had yet another vital advantage. A rare bird among politicians, and especially among residents of the White House, he was not especially sensitive or attentive to Jewish voices and lobbies... As it turned out, it was this kind of President—George [H. W.] Bush in the late 1980s is another case in point—who was ready to confront Israel head on and overlook the sensibilities of her friends in America that managed eventually to produce meaningful breakthroughs on the way to an Arab-Israeli peace." Read that again. From an Israeli foreign minister. The presidents who ignored the lobby are the ones who made peace. The presidents who listened to the lobby did not. Ben-Ami is not some critic of Israel. He was a key participant at Camp David in 2000. He served as Israel foreign minister. He is saying this on the record. that is the proof that destroys the lobby's whole story. The lobby says it protects Israel. It says without the lobby America would abandon Israel. But look at history. Carter made the only Arab-Israeli peace treaty that has lasted. He did it by ignoring the lobby. Bush Sr. brought the Arabs to the table by pressuring Israel. He did it by confronting the lobby. Every president who listened to the lobby, from Clinton to Bush Jr., promised peace and delivered occupation. The lobby does not produce peace. It produces the exact opposite. And the people who made peace are the ones the lobby fought. That is not a coincidence. That is the whole answer in one comparison. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine
